# Stocking frame (knitting machine) (`knitting_frame`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs wire_drawing; helped by textile_fibres, precision_measurement
- Core idea: Knitting makes cloth from one thread by pulling loops through loops, which gives a stretchy fabric for stockings. The frame has a row of fixed hooked needles, one for each stitch, each hook ending in a springy tip (the beard) that can be pressed into a groove in the shank. The thread is laid across the needles; thin plates between them push it into a loop on every needle; a bar presses all the beards shut, so the old row of loops slides over the closed hooks and off, leaving the new loops hanging through them. One pass makes a whole row, ten or more times faster than hand knitting. A frame has over two thousand parts and needs evenly made needles of springy wire.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying to copy the motion of two hand needles; the frame works on a different principle
  - Uneven or soft needles, which drop stitches
  - Repeating the tale that Queen Elizabeth refused Lee a patent to protect hand knitters; it first appears long afterwards and is not documented
- History: islamic: c. 11th–13th c. – hand-knitted cotton socks from Egypt, the oldest true knitting; europe: 13th–14th c. – hand knitting in Spain and Italy; 1589 (traditional date) William Lee's stocking frame, Nottinghamshire; he took it to Rouen c. 1610; 1758 Jedediah Strutt's rib attachment; 1775 warp knitting; 1811–1812 Luddite frame breaking; 1816 Marc Brunel's circular frame; 1847–1849 Matthew Townsend develops and patents latch needles
- Read:
  - William Felkin, A History of the Machine-Wrought Hosiery and Lace Manufactures (1867)
  - Richard L. Hills, William Lee and His Knitting Machine, Journal of the Textile Institute 80 (1989)
